items.stem: The riskiest-assumption test should target the belief that:

options.text: Is easiest and cheapest to confirm
options.rationale: Ease is not the criterion; risk to the whole idea is.

options.text: Would most damage the idea if it turned out to be false
options.rationale: Correct: testing the most dangerous assumption first saves wasted effort.

options.text: The founder is most confident about
options.rationale: High confidence does not mean high risk to test.
Investor interest is not the basis for choosing the first test.

items.explanation: Correct: testing the most dangerous assumption first saves wasted effort.

items.stem: A customer interview question is 'leading' when it:

options.text: Asks about a past behaviour in detail
options.rationale: Asking about real past behaviour is good practice.

options.text: Signals the answer the founder hopes to hear
options.rationale: Correct: leading questions nudge the interviewee toward a desired answer.
Open, neutral questions are the opposite of leading.
Exploring workarounds reveals real needs; it is not leading.

items.explanation: Correct: leading questions nudge the interviewee toward a desired answer.

items.stem: Which TWO are signs of a 'vanity metric' rather than real traction? (Select TWO)

options.text: A number that always goes up and never informs a decision
options.rationale: Correct: a metric that cannot change a decision adds no learning.

options.text: Total registered sign-ups with no active use
options.rationale: Correct: sign-ups without activation can overstate demand.

options.text: Repeat purchases by the same customers
options.rationale: Repeat purchase is a meaningful sign of value.
Retention is a strong, decision-relevant metric.

items.explanation: Correct: a metric that cannot change a decision adds no learning.; Correct: sign-ups without activation can overstate demand.
